disease.name: Common Cold
disease.scientific_name: Acute Viral Upper Respiratory Tract Infection

overview.summary: The common cold is a syndrome of familiar upper respiratory symptoms caused by any one of more than 200 respiratory viruses. It is the most common human disease and, because of the large number of causative viruses, one of the most complex. It is self-diagnosing, self-treating, and self-limiting — most episodes resolve within 7–10 days. Despite its mildness, it carries enormous economic and social burden through missed work, school absences, and over-the-counter medicine expenditure.

global_burden.reason_for_missed_work: one of the leading causes of work absenteeism

iceberg_concept.description: The common cold sits in the middle of the viral infection spectrum — above asymptomatic infection but below severe respiratory illness such as pneumonia or flu-like illness. Most respiratory virus infections result in sub-clinical or asymptomatic infection not noticed by the host. The cold represents the visible tip of a large iceberg of respiratory virus infection.
spectrum_ascending_severity: asymptomatic infection (most common — 69–74% of positive samples in studies)
iceberg_concept.study_evidence: A study of 214 healthy individuals aged 3–63 years collected nasopharyngeal swabs twice weekly for two years. Of 4,215 samples, 737 tested positive for one or multiple respiratory viruses. Among positive results, 69–74% were classified as asymptomatic.

anatomy_and_physiology.overview: The common cold is a syndrome of symptoms caused by the innate immune response to viral infection of the upper respiratory tract epithelium, not by direct tissue damage from the virus itself. Symptoms vary from person to person and depend on the infecting virus and the host's immune response.

viral_entry.rhinovirus_entry: Epithelial cells of the nasopharynx carry intercellular adhesion molecule-1 (ICAM-1) receptors. Rhinovirus binds these receptors to enter cells. Nasal epithelial cells do NOT have these receptors — explaining why rhinovirus causes minimal nasal mucosa destruction but consistent nasopharyngeal damage.
viral_entry.other_viruses: Different viruses use different entry mechanisms and receptors

inflammatory_cascade.step_1: Virus infects respiratory epithelium and replicates
inflammatory_cascade.step_2: Pattern Recognition Receptors (PRRs) detect viral RNA or DNA
inflammatory_cascade.step_4: Release of cytokines: interferons, IL-6, IL-8, TNF-alpha
inflammatory_cascade.step_5: Recruitment of immune cells (neutrophils, macrophages, lymphocytes)
inflammatory_cascade.step_6: Local inflammatory mediators generated: bradykinin, prostaglandins
inflammatory_cascade.step_7: Nasal blood vessel dilation, mucosal oedema, increased secretion
inflammatory_cascade.step_8: Systemic cytokine circulation producing fever, headache, myalgia, fatigue

nasal_mucosa_changes.rhinovirus_infection: Characterised by oedema and hyperaemia with transudative rhinorrhoea, WITHOUT direct damage to the columnar epithelium
nasal_mucosa_changes.influenza_contrast: Influenza, adenoviruses, and parainfluenza viruses cause more severe cytopathic effects on respiratory epithelium
sequence: Separation of epithelial cells by oedema fluid
Surface cells loosen and slough off
Entire epithelium may disintegrate in severe cases
Cell regeneration begins from basement membrane

mucopurulent_discharge.appearance: Yellow or green nasal discharge is NORMAL as the cold progresses
mucopurulent_discharge.cause: Influx of neutrophils and macrophages; does NOT indicate bacterial infection requiring antibiotics
mucopurulent_discharge.clinical_implication: Presence of coloured mucus is not a reason to prescribe antibiotics

eustachian_tube_effects.findings: 2 days after rhinoviral infection, eustachian tube function was reduced to 50% of usual potency in studies
eustachian_tube_effects.middle_ear_effect: 20% of infected persons had significant pressure changes in the middle ear
eustachian_tube_effects.implication: Creates conditions for secondary bacterial otitis media

types.name: Rhinovirus (HRV)
types.classification: Species A, B, C with more than 100 serotypes
types.frequency_of_colds: more than 50% of all adult colds
types.severity: usually mild, rarely causes lower respiratory disease in healthy adults
notes: Most common cause of common cold worldwide
More than 100 serotypes identified
Can be considered the most common infection of humans globally
Enters cells via ICAM-1 receptor on nasopharyngeal epithelium
Causes minimal nasal mucosa disruption but consistent nasopharyngeal damage
In children, a significant trigger for asthma exacerbations

types.name: Seasonal Coronavirus
notes: Produces clinical picture similar to rhinovirus
More likely to produce myalgias, headaches, and malaise than rhinoviruses
More commonly produces fever than rhinovirus
With increasing immunity to SARS-CoV-2 worldwide, COVID-19 may eventually evolve to cause a common cold-like illness

types.name: Respiratory Syncytial Virus
notes: Causes mild cold-like symptoms in older children and adults
A major cause of bronchiolitis and lower respiratory tract infections in infants under 2 years
RSV type A associated with more severe infections
In 2015, estimated 33.1 million episodes globally in children under 5, causing 3.2 million hospital admissions and over 11,800 deaths
Significant cause of morbidity and mortality in the elderly (estimated 1.2 million deaths in elderly from RSV and other respiratory viruses in 2015)
Immunity to RSV is short-lived, explaining repeated infections throughout life
RSV vaccine (Abrysvo) was approved by FDA in May 2023 for individuals 60 years and older

types.name: Parainfluenza Virus
notes: Causes croup and bronchiolitis pattern in young children
Milder cold symptoms in older individuals and adults
Produces more fever than rhinovirus or RSV
12% of isolates in younger population, 2–7.5% in older population in studies

types.name: Influenza Virus
notes: Usually produces a pattern of respiratory illness distinctly different from the common cold
Flu causes high fever, headache, body aches — unlike the milder nasal-centred cold
Third most common cause in some community studies
Key clinical distinction: influenza has high fever and myalgia; cold does not

types.name: Adenovirus
types.serotypes: 41 recognized serotypes with more than 100 subtypes
notes: Well known for producing conjunctivitis and laryngitis alongside cold symptoms
Types 3 and 7 cause pharyngoconjunctival fever — severe conjunctivitis and pharyngitis with minor cold symptoms
Pharyngoconjunctival fever most often found in summer when swimming in non-chlorinated pools
Genetic heterogeneity of adenoviruses makes population studies difficult

types.name: Human Metapneumovirus
notes: Discovered in 2001 by researchers in the Netherlands in stored nasopharyngeal samples from children
Had been in circulation for approximately 65 years before discovery
Nearly every child is infected by age 5
Can cause severe lower respiratory illness in infants and immunocompromised individuals

types.name: Human Bocavirus
notes: Discovered in 2005 from nasopharyngeal samples in children
Shown to cause common cold in children

types.name: Echovirus
notes: Causes coryza — acute rhinitis with minimal other symptoms
Associated with summer cold-like episodes

types.name: Coxsackievirus
notes: Well known for causing epidemic cervical myalgia, pleurisy, hand-foot-mouth disease, and herpangina alongside respiratory infections
Coxsackievirus type A21 can be transmitted via airborne droplets across a room
Associated with summer cold outbreaks

types.name: SARS-CoV-2 (Pandemic Coronavirus)
notes: Can cause cold-like symptoms especially with high population immunity
Pandemic caused by SARS-CoV-2 led to a revolution in respiratory virus research
With increased global immunity, COVID-19 may evolve toward a common cold pattern

types.name: Enterovirus D68
notes: Associated with respiratory illness and potential severe neurological complications
Listed by CDC as a cause of cold-like symptoms in the United States

causes.note: All known respiratory viruses are able to produce the illness complex recognised as the common cold.

transmission.primary: direct hand-to-hand contact — transfer of virus from infected person's hands to mucous membranes of susceptible person
transmission.tertiary: inhalation of respiratory aerosol droplets from coughing or sneezing within close range
transmission.droplet_route: possible when infected person coughs or sneezes and recipient is within a few feet
transmission.kissing: low risk — only 1 of 16 susceptible recipients infected in a study of 1.5-minute kisses; saliva has little detectable virus 90% of the time
transmission.recirculated_air: studies of commercial airliners show no difference in cold incidence with recirculated vs fresh air ventilation

contagiousness_period.peak: second day of illness when viral shedding is highest
contagiousness_period.duration: low level viral shedding may persist for up to 2 weeks
contagiousness_period.incubation_note: virus present in nasal washings during incubation period before symptoms begin

incubation_period.note: Symptoms usually show up approximately 2 days after a person becomes infected

common_symptoms.details: Initially clear and watery during first 2 days, then becomes more viscous and mucopurulent. The most common symptom of the common cold.
common_symptoms.mechanism: Bradykinin-induced nasal blood vessel dilation and increased glandular secretion

common_symptoms.details: Stuffiness due to swelling and oedema of the nasal mucosa. Second most common symptom.
common_symptoms.mechanism: Inflammatory mediators causing vasodilatation and mucosal swelling

common_symptoms.details: Often one of the earliest symptoms, frequently occurring in the first 1–2 days
common_symptoms.mechanism: Bradykinin and prostaglandin stimulation of nasal nerve endings

common_symptoms.details: Common early symptom, typically mild. Often the very first sign of a developing cold. Decreases after day 2–3.
common_symptoms.mechanism: Bradykinin activating pain nerve endings in the throat

common_symptoms.details: Usually mild; caused mainly by nasal obstruction and postnasal drip stimulating upper airway cough receptors. In young children RSV and parainfluenza can cause cough by direct lower respiratory tract invasion.
common_symptoms.mechanism: Postnasal drip stimulation of pharyngeal cough receptors; prostaglandins increase cough reflex sensitivity

common_symptoms.details: Common, especially in early cold. More severe headache may suggest influenza.
common_symptoms.mechanism: Prostaglandin E2 mediates headache; cytokine-induced systemic inflammation

common_symptoms.details: Temperature below 38°C (100.4°F). Uncommon in adults but may be present in children. High fever is NOT typical of the common cold — it suggests influenza or another diagnosis.
common_symptoms.mechanism: Cytokine IL-6, IL-8, TNF-alpha stimulate prostaglandin-mediated fever

common_symptoms.symptom: Mild body aches and muscle pain (myalgia)
common_symptoms.details: Mild muscle and joint aches. Severe myalgia is more characteristic of influenza.
common_symptoms.mechanism: Cytokine-induced systemic inflammation; prostaglandin E2 mediates muscle pain

common_symptoms.details: Feeling of illness and lethargy
common_symptoms.mechanism: Systemic cytokine effects including IL-6 and TNF-alpha

common_symptoms.details: May appear early in the illness; virus can travel via tear ducts from eyes into nasal cavity
common_symptoms.mechanism: Inflammatory response in conjunctiva

common_symptoms.details: Reduced desire to eat during active illness
common_symptoms.mechanism: Cytokine-mediated appetite suppression

common_symptoms.details: Mucus dripping down the back of the throat; often contributes to persistent cough and throat clearing
common_symptoms.mechanism: Excess mucus production combined with impaired mucociliary clearance

mechanism_of_symptoms.overview: Viral infection of the upper respiratory tract triggers a local innate immune response in the infected epithelium. This response generates all the symptoms of the common cold through two pathways: systemic cytokine-mediated symptoms and local inflammatory mediator-driven symptoms.

systemic_pathway.trigger: Pattern Recognition Receptors (PRRs) on epithelial cells and immune cells detect viral DNA and RNA

local_pathway.bradykinin_mechanism: Generated by release of kallikrein enzyme from epithelial cells converting kininogen to bradykinin. Acts on blood vessels and nerves.
local_pathway.prostaglandin_mechanism: Arachidonic acid released from membrane phospholipids by viral infection is converted to prostaglandins by cyclooxygenase enzymes. Prostaglandin E2 is most common.
local_pathway.important_note: Histamine is NOT a major mediator of common cold symptoms — unlike in allergic rhinitis. Kinins are more closely associated with cold symptoms than histamine. This explains why non-sedating antihistamines are ineffective for colds.

mechanism_of_symptoms.prodromal_symptoms: The first signs of a cold include throat irritation, sneezing, chilliness, mild fever, and tiredness — symptoms that may become more severe as infection progresses.

asymptomatic_infection.definition: Subclinical infection — person is infected with virus but shows no symptoms
asymptomatic_infection.also_possible: Exposure to cold viruses without becoming infected at all
asymptomatic_infection.study_data: In a 2-year study, 69–74% of positive respiratory virus samples from healthy individuals were classified as asymptomatic

risk_factors.overview: The common cold is influenced by many biological, behavioural, environmental, and social factors. Risk factors affect both the incidence (how often you get colds) and the severity (how bad they are).

factors_increasing_incidence.details: Infants and children have undeveloped immune systems and have not yet acquired immunity through previous exposures. School-age children have 6–8 colds per year versus 2–4 for adults. Children in daycare or school settings have markedly increased exposure.
factors_increasing_incidence.mechanism: Immature immune system; no prior exposure to the many rhinovirus serotypes

factors_increasing_incidence.details: Long-term psychological stress negatively impacts the immune system and mucosal immunity. Studies show a moderate correlation between stressful life events and incidence of common cold. A 1-year study of 1,149 subjects aged 23–68 found psychological stress was a risk factor.
factors_increasing_incidence.mechanism: Stress suppresses secretory immunoglobulin A (sIgA); cortisol release may compromise immune response

factors_increasing_incidence.details: Poor sleep quality is an important predictor of cold susceptibility. Subjects with less than 7 hours of sleep were almost three times more likely to develop a cold than those with 8 or more hours, confirmed in multiple studies.
factors_increasing_incidence.mechanism: Sleep deprivation decreases mitogen proliferation of lymphocytes and affects multiple immune markers

factors_increasing_incidence.details: Spending time in crowds — underground trains, supermarkets, theatres, cinemas, restaurants, parties — increases risk of circulating respiratory infections. Paradoxically, very sociable persons may have greater resistance than introverted persons despite more exposures, though the mechanism is unknown.
factors_increasing_incidence.mechanism: Direct contact and close proximity facilitates viral transmission

factors_increasing_incidence.details: Smokers are more likely to develop infections after virus exposure and also more likely to develop illness compared to non-smokers. Smoking increases risk of respiratory infection.
factors_increasing_incidence.mechanism: Damages respiratory epithelium; alters structural, functional, and immunological host defences

factors_increasing_incidence.factor: Children in household or daycare settings
factors_increasing_incidence.details: Exposure to young children in daycare settings significantly increases cold risk. Women are almost twice as likely to develop a cold as men when children in the family are sick, because women have more contact with children.
factors_increasing_incidence.mechanism: Children are major virus shedders; close household contact increases transmission

factors_increasing_incidence.factor: No prior immunity to specific serotype
factors_increasing_incidence.details: Adults have fewer colds than children because they have accumulated partial immunity through exposure to many rhinovirus serotypes. However, with over 100 rhinovirus serotypes, complete immunity is never achieved.
factors_increasing_incidence.mechanism: Antibody-mediated protection against specific serotypes; each infection induces short-lived serotype-specific immunity

factors_increasing_incidence.details: More symptomatic infections in winter and during rainy season in tropics. People spend more time indoors in closer contact; cold inspired air may also slow mucociliary clearance and leukocyte activity.
factors_increasing_incidence.mechanism: Indoor crowding; cold air impairs local nasal defences; lower vitamin D in winter

factors_increasing_incidence.details: Deficiency of calories, protein, vitamins C and D, and minerals impairs general health and immune function. Malnourished children in developing countries are particularly susceptible to respiratory infection morbidity and mortality.
factors_increasing_incidence.mechanism: Nutrients support epithelial integrity and immune cell function

factors_increasing_severity: asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)

controversial_factor_cold_exposure.folk_belief: Getting chilled, going outside with wet hair, or getting caught in the rain causes colds
controversial_factor_cold_exposure.scientific_evidence: Laboratory experiments involving challenge with cold viruses and chilling have failed to demonstrate any effect of cold exposure on susceptibility to infection. Cold temperatures do NOT directly cause colds.
controversial_factor_cold_exposure.nuanced_explanation: There is a proposed mechanism: chilling of the body surface causes intense ischaemia and cooling of the pharynx and tonsils. This reflex vasoconstriction may reduce resistance to infection, potentially converting a subclinical infection into a symptomatic one. More people catch colds in cold weather because they spend more time indoors in prolonged contact with infected people — not because of the cold itself.
controversial_factor_cold_exposure.conclusion: Cold temperatures do not directly cause the common cold. The virus must be present.

alcohol_note.evidence: Moderate alcohol consumption (up to 3–4 drinks/day) was associated with decreased risk of developing a cold in non-smokers in one study. Moderate alcohol may have a beneficial effect on the immune system.
alcohol_note.caution: This does not constitute a recommendation to consume alcohol as prevention

clinical_diagnosis.basis: Symptoms and observed signs — no laboratory tests required for typical uncomplicated cases
physical_examination_findings: Swelling and congestion of nasal passages
Redness of the throat (mild, without exudate)
Possible enlarged lymph nodes in the neck
clinical_diagnosis.chest_xray: NOT needed unless chest exam is abnormal or pneumonia is suspected

conditions_that_mimic_cold.differentiator: Cough or sore throat usually NOT seen with allergies; itching is more prominent; symptoms are recurrent and triggered by allergens
Nasal congestion and drainage NOT generally seen; high fever; exudate on tonsils
Usually associated with significant facial pain and purulent nasal discharge lasting beyond 10 days without improvement
High fever (38–40°C), severe myalgia, headache, and rapid onset distinguish flu from cold. Rapid influenza test during flu season can confirm.
conditions_that_mimic_cold.rule: During flu season, obtain nasal swabs for rapid flu testing

conditions_that_mimic_cold.differentiator: Associated with prolonged coughing, sometimes with vomiting; characteristic whoop sound
May be indistinguishable from common cold especially with high immunity; testing required if antiviral treatment eligibility is relevant
Non-infectious, triggered by environmental factors; no fever, no infectious prodrome

laboratory_testing.when_indicated: Routine laboratory testing is NOT recommended for uncomplicated common cold
special_circumstances: Rapid influenza antigen test when influenza is suspected during flu season
Rapid RSV test for high-risk infants under 2 years with compatible symptoms
COVID-19 testing when antiviral treatment may be indicated
C-reactive protein (CRP) can help distinguish viral (CRP <20 mg/L) from bacterial infection (CRP >40 mg/L)

nucleic_acid_PCR.use: reference labs, research, returned travellers, low parasitaemia

serology.use: IgG antibody testing — can be done any time, not just during acute illness

tissue_culture.gold_standard_role: viral culture remains important gold standard despite advances in antigen detection

treatment.principle: No cure exists for the common cold. No vaccines are currently available for the common cold. Treatments aim to relieve symptoms while the immune system clears the infection. The illness is self-limiting and will resolve on its own.

antibiotics.reason: Antibiotics work against bacteria, NOT viruses. They do not kill viruses and provide no benefit for uncomplicated colds.
risks_of_unnecessary_antibiotics: allergic reactions ranging from mild rash to severe anaphylaxis
Clostridioides difficile (C. diff) infection causing serious diarrhoea
GI symptoms including nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea
contribution to antibiotic resistance in community
antibiotics.exception: Antibiotics are appropriate only if a secondary bacterial infection develops (e.g., bacterial sinusitis, pneumonia, bacterial otitis media)

antiviral_therapy.common_cold_viruses: There are currently no antivirals that work against rhinoviruses or other common respiratory viruses causing cold symptoms
antiviral_therapy.covid_19: If COVID-19 is diagnosed, antiviral treatment (e.g., nirmatrelvir/ritonavir) may be available and should be started within 5–7 days of symptom onset
antiviral_therapy.influenza: Antivirals for flu work best when started within 2 days of symptom onset
antiviral_therapy.note: Contact healthcare provider promptly if symptoms could be COVID-19 or flu in high-risk patients

analgesics_antipyretics.paracetamol_dose: 500–1000 mg every 4–6 hours as needed while awake, with water (max 4000 mg/day)
analgesics_antipyretics.ibuprofen_dose: 200–400 mg every 6–8 hours as needed with small snack (max 1200 mg/day)
analgesics_antipyretics.ibuprofen_avoid_in: persons over 65, pregnant women, severe liver or kidney disease, peptic ulcer disease, heart failure, history of stroke, GERD, IBD, liver cirrhosis
analgesics_antipyretics.aspirin_note: Aspirin reduces some cold symptoms but increases viral shedding duration; not recommended in children due to Reye's syndrome risk

nasal_decongestants_topical.mechanism: Constrict nasal blood vessels, reducing mucosal swelling
nasal_decongestants_topical.critical_warning: Limit use to 2–3 days — rebound congestion (rhinitis medicamentosa) occurs after 72 hours of use; the congestion may worsen. Can also cause nosebleeds, agitation, insomnia, and worsened hypertension.
nasal_decongestants_topical.reasons_for_infant_contraindication: Risk of serious CNS effects ranging from sedation to convulsive attacks resembling seizures in infants and young children

nasal_decongestants_oral.efficacy: Pseudoephedrine effective; phenylephrine (common OTC ingredient) is NOT very effective
nasal_decongestants_oral.pseudoephedrine_note: Purchase limited due to use in manufacture of amphetamine drugs

first_generation.benefit: Modest benefit for sneezing and runny nose in adults
first_generation.mechanism_of_limited_benefit: Rhinorrhoea in colds is mediated by kinins, not histamine — antihistamines are not targeting the primary mediator
first_generation.antihistamine_for_cough: Thought to act indirectly by reducing postnasal drip
first_generation.note: Antihistamines may be helpful in adolescents and adults; NOT recommended in young children

second_generation.efficacy_for_cold: NOT effective for common cold symptoms
second_generation.reason: Second-generation antihistamines do not have the same anticholinergic properties; histamine is not the main mediator of cold symptoms

cromolyn_sodium.benefit: May relieve runny nose, cough, and sneezing

dextromethorphan.evidence: Conflicting results; more effective than codeine in studies
dextromethorphan.indication: May provide relief when persistent cough disrupts sleep or feeding
dextromethorphan.not_needed: Cough suppression is usually not needed; cough reflex is a protective mechanism

antitussives_cough_suppressants.antihistamines_for_cough: May reduce cough through drying effect on mucosa and reduction of postnasal drip

guaifenesin.evidence: One RCT in 65 young adults showed no change in cough or sputum thickness
guaifenesin.note: Despite popularity, evidence of benefit is limited

ipratropium_bromide_nasal_spray.evidence: 5 RCTs in adults showed significant symptom relief, especially for excessive nasal discharge and sneezing

lozenges.evidence: Some studies show reduction in duration and severity of cold symptoms when taken within 24 hours of symptom onset
lozenges.critical_warning: Intranasal zinc products have been associated with PERMANENT loss of smell — CONTRAINDICATED as nasal products
lozenges.child_evidence: Studies in children taking zinc sulfate decreased cold rate, but adult studies are inconsistent

vitamin_c.prevention: Does NOT reduce cold incidence in the general population — routine supplementation NOT justified
vitamin_c.treatment: If started after onset of cold symptoms, does NOT reduce symptom severity or duration
vitamin_c.regular_supplementation: May slightly reduce duration of colds if taken regularly before illness onset
vitamin_c.background: Claims that vitamin C prevents and cures colds were popularised by Nobel laureate Linus Pauling in 1970; later large meta-analyses found no benefit for prevention

vitamin_d.evidence: Controversial. Some reports show no benefit; others report benefit especially in vitamin D deficient individuals

echinacea.evidence: Two of the most popular herbal treatments with some support from clinical trials. Clinical relevance of efficacy has been questioned by Cochrane reviews. Some support from RCTs.

pelargonium.evidence: Some support from clinical trials for acute cough due to lower respiratory tract infection

iota_carrageenan.claimed_benefit: Antiviral medicine for common cold; studied in several clinical trials

intranasal_glucocorticoids.evidence: NOT effective for common cold symptoms; ARE effective for allergic rhinitis

age_restriction_otc.rule: Over-the-counter cough and cold medicines are NOT recommended for children younger than 6 years old
age_restriction_otc.reason: Can result in serious and sometimes life-threatening side effects
age_restriction_otc.US_FDA_position: OTC cough/cold medicines not recommended for children under 6

fever_treatment_children.instruction: Contact healthcare provider about correct dose; read and follow all directions
fever_treatment_children.age_restriction_ibuprofen: Avoid in infants under 6 months without medical guidance

symptomatic_treatments_children.codeine_in_children: NOT recommended — risk of respiratory depression and narcotic dependency
symptomatic_treatments_children.topical_decongestants_infants: CONTRAINDICATED — risk of serious CNS effects including convulsions

honey_for_cough.efficacy: Safe and effective for cough relief in children 1 year and older
honey_for_cough.contraindication: Babies under 1 year should NOT be given honey — risk of infant botulism

symptomatic_treatments_children.combination_products: Combination products containing topical anaesthetic agents, mucolytics, antihistamines, oral decongestants, antitussives, and anticholinergics should be avoided in young children. The American Academy of Pediatrics advises against use of combination cough and cold remedies.

rest.recommendation: Get plenty of sleep. Adjust sleeping position to prop head up with pillows to help mucus drainage.
rest.rationale: Sleep is critical for immune function; adults with less than 7 hours sleep are nearly 3 times more likely to develop a cold

fluids.recommendation: Drink plenty of fluids — 8 glasses per day. Water and fruit juice are ideal. Warm fluids such as tea and soups are especially soothing.
fluids.honey_addition: Adding honey can relieve sore throats and coughs in adults and children over 1 year

humidifier.recommendation: Use a cool-mist humidifier or vaporizer to increase air moisture and ease breathing
humidifier.warning: Breathe some steamy air but NOT hot steam directly — hot steam can damage nasal passages and cause burns

saline_nasal.drops_and_sprays: Saline nose drops or sprays are safe and effective for clearing congestion, especially in infants and young children
saline_nasal.gargling: Gargling with salt water can help clear mucus and soothe sore throats — mix half teaspoon of salt in 8 ounces of warm water
saline_nasal.suction_bulb: For young children, use a rubber suction bulb to clear mucus from nasal passages

throat_lozenges.recommendation: Use throat lozenges or cough drops for sore throat relief
throat_lozenges.age_restriction: Do not give lozenges to children younger than 4 years old — aspiration risk

supportive_home_care.diet: Eat a healthy diet high in fresh fruits (berries, citrus) and vegetables (leafy greens, peppers, carrots) to support immune function
supportive_home_care.smoking: Limit smoking or vaping — these worsen symptoms and delay recovery

steam_inhalation.sitting_in_steam_shower: Sitting in a bathroom with steam from a running shower may relieve congestion
steam_inhalation.hot_steam_inhalation: NOT recommended — hot steam can damage nasal mucosa; double-blind RCT showed breathing steam demonstrated increased airway resistance and fourfold increase in side effects

chicken_soup.tradition: Reported positive effects attributed to mucolytic effects of vapours from hot soup; may also stimulate nasal mucus production and loosen respiratory secretions
chicken_soup.evidence: Traditional use and soothing effect support recommending warm teas or soups

treatment_categories.before_cold_immune_support: Vitamins, minerals, probiotics, herbal medicines — evidence for most is limited; market valued over $20 billion USD in 2021
treatment_categories.at_first_signs_antiviral: No proven over-the-counter antiviral for common cold viruses available
treatment_categories.during_cold_symptom_relief: Main category of treatment; see symptomatic treatments above

analgesics_antipyretics.paracetamol_dose: 500–1000 mg every 4–6 hours as needed while awake, with water (max 4000 mg/day)
analgesics_antipyretics.ibuprofen_dose: 200–400 mg every 6–8 hours as needed with small snack (max 1200 mg/day)
analgesics_antipyretics.ibuprofen_avoid_in: persons over 65, pregnant women, severe liver or kidney disease, peptic ulcer disease, heart failure, history of stroke, GERD, IBD, liver cirrhosis
analgesics_antipyretics.aspirin_note: Aspirin reduces some cold symptoms but increases viral shedding duration; not recommended in children due to Reye's syndrome risk

nasal_decongestants_topical.mechanism: Constrict nasal blood vessels, reducing mucosal swelling
nasal_decongestants_topical.critical_warning: Limit use to 2–3 days — rebound congestion (rhinitis medicamentosa) occurs after 72 hours of use; the congestion may worsen. Can also cause nosebleeds, agitation, insomnia, and worsened hypertension.
nasal_decongestants_topical.reasons_for_infant_contraindication: Risk of serious CNS effects ranging from sedation to convulsive attacks resembling seizures in infants and young children

nasal_decongestants_oral.efficacy: Pseudoephedrine effective; phenylephrine (common OTC ingredient) is NOT very effective
nasal_decongestants_oral.pseudoephedrine_note: Purchase limited due to use in manufacture of amphetamine drugs

first_generation.benefit: Modest benefit for sneezing and runny nose in adults
first_generation.mechanism_of_limited_benefit: Rhinorrhoea in colds is mediated by kinins, not histamine — antihistamines are not targeting the primary mediator
first_generation.antihistamine_for_cough: Thought to act indirectly by reducing postnasal drip
first_generation.note: Antihistamines may be helpful in adolescents and adults; NOT recommended in young children

second_generation.efficacy_for_cold: NOT effective for common cold symptoms
second_generation.reason: Second-generation antihistamines do not have the same anticholinergic properties; histamine is not the main mediator of cold symptoms

cromolyn_sodium.benefit: May relieve runny nose, cough, and sneezing

dextromethorphan.evidence: Conflicting results; more effective than codeine in studies
dextromethorphan.indication: May provide relief when persistent cough disrupts sleep or feeding
dextromethorphan.not_needed: Cough suppression is usually not needed; cough reflex is a protective mechanism

antitussives_cough_suppressants.antihistamines_for_cough: May reduce cough through drying effect on mucosa and reduction of postnasal drip

guaifenesin.evidence: One RCT in 65 young adults showed no change in cough or sputum thickness
guaifenesin.note: Despite popularity, evidence of benefit is limited

ipratropium_bromide_nasal_spray.evidence: 5 RCTs in adults showed significant symptom relief, especially for excessive nasal discharge and sneezing

lozenges.evidence: Some studies show reduction in duration and severity of cold symptoms when taken within 24 hours of symptom onset
lozenges.critical_warning: Intranasal zinc products have been associated with PERMANENT loss of smell — CONTRAINDICATED as nasal products
lozenges.child_evidence: Studies in children taking zinc sulfate decreased cold rate, but adult studies are inconsistent

vitamin_c.prevention: Does NOT reduce cold incidence in the general population — routine supplementation NOT justified
vitamin_c.treatment: If started after onset of cold symptoms, does NOT reduce symptom severity or duration
vitamin_c.regular_supplementation: May slightly reduce duration of colds if taken regularly before illness onset
vitamin_c.background: Claims that vitamin C prevents and cures colds were popularised by Nobel laureate Linus Pauling in 1970; later large meta-analyses found no benefit for prevention

vitamin_d.evidence: Controversial. Some reports show no benefit; others report benefit especially in vitamin D deficient individuals

echinacea.evidence: Two of the most popular herbal treatments with some support from clinical trials. Clinical relevance of efficacy has been questioned by Cochrane reviews. Some support from RCTs.

pelargonium.evidence: Some support from clinical trials for acute cough due to lower respiratory tract infection

iota_carrageenan.claimed_benefit: Antiviral medicine for common cold; studied in several clinical trials

intranasal_glucocorticoids.evidence: NOT effective for common cold symptoms; ARE effective for allergic rhinitis

rest.recommendation: Get plenty of sleep. Adjust sleeping position to prop head up with pillows to help mucus drainage.
rest.rationale: Sleep is critical for immune function; adults with less than 7 hours sleep are nearly 3 times more likely to develop a cold

fluids.recommendation: Drink plenty of fluids — 8 glasses per day. Water and fruit juice are ideal. Warm fluids such as tea and soups are especially soothing.
fluids.honey_addition: Adding honey can relieve sore throats and coughs in adults and children over 1 year

humidifier.recommendation: Use a cool-mist humidifier or vaporizer to increase air moisture and ease breathing
humidifier.warning: Breathe some steamy air but NOT hot steam directly — hot steam can damage nasal passages and cause burns

saline_nasal.drops_and_sprays: Saline nose drops or sprays are safe and effective for clearing congestion, especially in infants and young children
saline_nasal.gargling: Gargling with salt water can help clear mucus and soothe sore throats — mix half teaspoon of salt in 8 ounces of warm water
saline_nasal.suction_bulb: For young children, use a rubber suction bulb to clear mucus from nasal passages

throat_lozenges.recommendation: Use throat lozenges or cough drops for sore throat relief
throat_lozenges.age_restriction: Do not give lozenges to children younger than 4 years old — aspiration risk

diet_and_nutrition.diet: Eat a healthy diet high in fresh fruits (berries, citrus) and vegetables (leafy greens, peppers, carrots) to support immune function
diet_and_nutrition.smoking: Limit smoking or vaping — these worsen symptoms and delay recovery

steam_inhalation.sitting_in_steam_shower: Sitting in a bathroom with steam from a running shower may relieve congestion
steam_inhalation.hot_steam_inhalation: NOT recommended — hot steam can damage nasal mucosa; double-blind RCT showed breathing steam demonstrated increased airway resistance and fourfold increase in side effects

chicken_soup.tradition: Reported positive effects attributed to mucolytic effects of vapours from hot soup; may also stimulate nasal mucus production and loosen respiratory secretions
chicken_soup.evidence: Traditional use and soothing effect support recommending warm teas or soups

prevention.overview: No vaccine is currently available for the common cold. Prevention relies on hygiene measures to interrupt transmission, general immune health practices, and reducing exposure to infectious contacts.

handwashing.recommendation: Frequent handwashing with soap and water — the single most effective preventive measure
handwashing.rationale: Rhinovirus recovered from 40–90% of hands of persons with colds; virus can survive on hands for at least 2 hours
handwashing.alternative: Alcohol-based hand sanitiser when soap and water unavailable (though studies show alcohol gels may be less effective when virus spreads by aerosol route)

avoiding_face_touching.recommendation: Avoid touching eyes, nose, and mouth with unwashed hands
avoiding_face_touching.reason: These are the entry routes for cold viruses into the body; virus can reach the nose when eyes are rubbed because tear ducts connect eyes to nasal cavity

respiratory_etiquette.recommendation: Cough and sneeze into your elbow or a tissue; dispose of tissues immediately
respiratory_etiquette.face_masks: Use face masks when sick or around sick contacts

avoiding_close_contact.recommendation: Avoid close contact with people who have a cold
avoiding_close_contact.crowded_places: Reduce time in crowded indoor spaces during cold season

surface_disinfection.recommendation: Disinfect commonly touched surfaces (phones, doorknobs, desks) with approved disinfectants
surface_disinfection.evidence: Iodine or phenol/alcohol disinfectants can interrupt transmission of rhinoviral infections in studies

prevention.not_sharing: Do NOT share food, drinks, utensils, or personal items with sick individuals

sleep.recommendation: Get 7–8 hours of sleep per night
sleep.evidence: Poor sleep quality is an important predictor of cold susceptibility; less than 7 hours of sleep nearly triples cold risk

prevention.stress_management: Manage chronic stress — prolonged psychological stress impairs mucosal and cellular immunity

diet_and_exercise.diet: Maintain a healthy diet rich in fruits and vegetables to support immune function
diet_and_exercise.exercise: Moderate exercise claimed to have beneficial effects on immune system and association with fewer sick days. However, a meta-analysis of 11 trials could not confirm this, and more research is needed. Severe exercise can INCREASE cold incidence in athletes.

vaccines.common_cold: No vaccine available for common cold — the large number of rhinovirus serotypes makes a universal vaccine impractical
vaccines.influenza: Annual influenza vaccination reduces flu-related respiratory illness; does NOT protect against rhinovirus or other cold viruses
vaccines.RSV_elderly: RSV vaccine (Abrysvo, mRESVIA) approved by FDA in May 2023 for adults 60 years and older
vaccines.RSV_infants: Nirsevimab (Beyfortus) monoclonal antibody recommended for infants and young children to prevent severe RSV infection
vaccines.vitamin_supplements: Regular supplementation with vitamins C, D, and E have NOT been shown to decrease incidence of colds in general population

travel_precautions.airline_travel: Studies show no difference in cold incidence with recirculated vs fresh air in commercial airliners — air conditioning is NOT a cause of colds

complications.overview: The common cold itself is of itself harmless in most cases, but bacterial invasion may follow the initial viral infection. These secondary invaders may produce disorders of serious consequence. All respiratory viruses are associated with causing common cold syndrome, but mild illness can develop into more serious lower respiratory tract infections.

complications_list.frequency: most common complication of the common cold
complications_list.mechanism: Cold causes problems with drainage and pressure regulation of the middle ear through eustachian tube dysfunction; allows secondary bacterial infection
complications_list.evidence: In one study, more than 90% of patients with otitis media had cold symptoms that were suspected to be virally induced; middle ear fluid contained culturable bacteria in 50–70% of cases

complications_list.mechanism: Viral sinusitis may be followed by secondary bacterial infection if mucociliary clearance is impaired
complications_list.note: Viral sinusitis (more common) will resolve within 3 weeks without antibiotics; bacterial sinusitis presents with worsening facial pain after initial improvement

complications_list.mechanism: Inflammation of the larynx (voice box) causing hoarseness or voice loss
Inflammation of the membrane lining the trachea (windpipe)
Inflammation of the bronchial membranes; may develop if virus spreads to lower airways

complications_list.frequency: mainly in infants under 2 years from RSV or parainfluenza
notes: RSV can infect lungs especially in children, older adults, and immunocompromised
In 2015: 33.1 million RSV-related episodes globally in children under 5, with 3.2 million hospital admissions and over 11,800 deaths

complications_list.mechanism: Barking cough and stridor from subglottic swelling
complications_list.cause: Primarily parainfluenza virus in young children

complications_list.note: Respiratory viruses previously believed restricted to upper airways are a common cause of lower respiratory infections

complications_list.frequency: rhinoviruses are a leading trigger for acute asthma attacks in children
complications_list.evidence: Rhinoviruses are responsible for considerable morbidity related to asthma exacerbation; airway hyperresponsiveness may persist up to 4 weeks post-infection
studies: Johnston SL et al (1995): community study in 9–11 year old children linking viral infections to asthma exacerbations
Tovey ER et al (2015): rhinoviruses significantly affect day-to-day respiratory symptoms in children with asthma

complications_list.mechanism: Respiratory viruses are major triggers for acute exacerbations of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and chronic bronchitis

serious_complication_warning_signs_requi: persistent high fever not responsive to paracetamol or ibuprofen
persistent or increasing shortness of breath
severe headache combined with neck pain or stiffness
dizziness, weakness, confusion, or constant lack of energy
signs_requiring_healthcare_provider_visi: coughing up thick grey or bloody sputum
development of even mild shortness of breath
worsening symptoms after a few days of getting better

infants_and_young_children.vulnerability: Infants start life with little immunity and high incidence of colds (6–10/year); maternal immunity from breast milk declines in first year

maternal_immunity.transfer: Immunoglobulins transferred via placenta and breast milk
maternal_immunity.duration: Declines in first year as infant ceases breastfeeding; immunoglobulins have relatively short half-life
maternal_immunity.covid_pandemic_effect: During COVID-19 pandemic, reduced circulation of common respiratory viruses led to lower antibody levels in maternal milk, contributing to RSV resurgence when restrictions were lifted

infants_and_young_children.otc_restrictions: OTC cough and cold medicines NOT recommended under 6 years due to serious side effect risk
treatment_options: paracetamol or ibuprofen for fever
saline nasal drops
honey for cough (over 1 year only)
fluids and rest
infants_and_young_children.complications_risk: Higher risk of otitis media, bronchiolitis, and croup

elderly.vulnerability: Waning immunity associated with old age leads to more severe outcomes from respiratory viruses
elderly.rsv_risk: RSV is a significant cause of morbidity and mortality in elderly, causing exacerbation of chronic respiratory and cardiac disease
elderly.mortality_risk: Elderly patients may die if cold-like symptoms are not distinguished from influenza

pregnant_women.treatment: Paracetamol is safe in all trimesters for symptom relief
pregnant_women.ibuprofen: Avoid in third trimester of pregnancy
pregnant_women.covid_flu_antivirals: Contact healthcare provider promptly if COVID-19 or flu is suspected — antiviral treatment may be available and is especially important in pregnancy

immunocompromised_patients.risk: Higher severity and risk of complications
immunocompromised_patients.common_cold_to_serious_illness: What is a mild cold in healthy individuals can progress to pneumonia or severe lower respiratory disease in immunocompromised patients

asthma_patients.rhinovirus_risk: Rhinovirus infection is a major trigger for acute asthma attacks in children
asthma_patients.airway_hyperresponsiveness: May persist up to 4 weeks after a cold
asthma_patients.management: Worsening asthma with colds requires healthcare provider visit

parenthood_effect.finding: Parenthood has been reported to DECREASE the chance of developing cold symptoms when challenged with a common cold virus. There was a clear increase in protection with having more children in the family.
parenthood_effect.mechanism: Unknown — the resistance was independent of pre-challenge viral-specific immunity, suggesting a non-antibody-mediated protective mechanism

medical_attention_signs: coughing up thick grey or bloody sputum
development of even mild shortness of breath
worsening symptoms after a few days of getting better

emergency_signs: chest pain
persistent high fever not responsive to paracetamol or ibuprofen
persistent or increasing shortness of breath
severe headache combined with neck pain or stiffness
dizziness, weakness, confusion, or constant lack of energy

disease_identity.name: Common Cold
disease_identity.definition: The common cold is a mild, self-limiting viral infection of the upper respiratory tract — including the nose, nasal passages, sinuses, throat (pharynx), larynx (voice box), and windpipe (trachea). It is caused by more than 200 different respiratory viruses and is the most frequent acute illness in humans worldwide.
disease_identity.nice_definition: A mild, self-limiting, upper respiratory tract infection characterized by nasal stuffiness and discharge, sneezing, sore throat, and cough.
disease_identity.etymology: The term 'common cold' has been in use for centuries. It was historically associated with the belief that exposure to cold temperatures caused the illness — a misconception that persisted until respiratory viruses such as rhinoviruses were identified in the 1950s as the true causative agents.
disease_identity.historical_note: The infectious cause of the common cold was formally recognised only after the 1950s discovery of rhinoviruses, providing the first scientific explanation for a disease that had been treated with theories of humoral imbalance, chilling, and miasma since ancient Greek times.

overview.summary: The common cold is a syndrome of familiar upper respiratory symptoms caused by any one of more than 200 respiratory viruses. It is the most common human disease and, because of the large number of causative viruses, one of the most complex. It is self-diagnosing, self-treating, and self-limiting — most episodes resolve within 7–10 days. Despite its mildness, it carries enormous economic and social burden through missed work, school absences, and over-the-counter medicine expenditure.

global_burden.reason_for_missed_work: one of the leading causes of work absenteeism

iceberg_concept.description: The common cold sits in the middle of the viral infection spectrum — above asymptomatic infection but below severe respiratory illness such as pneumonia or flu-like illness. Most respiratory virus infections result in sub-clinical or asymptomatic infection not noticed by the host. The cold represents the visible tip of a large iceberg of respiratory virus infection.
spectrum_ascending_severity: asymptomatic infection (most common — 69–74% of positive samples in studies)
iceberg_concept.study_evidence: A study of 214 healthy individuals aged 3–63 years collected nasopharyngeal swabs twice weekly for two years. Of 4,215 samples, 737 tested positive for one or multiple respiratory viruses. Among positive results, 69–74% were classified as asymptomatic.

causative_agents.note: All known respiratory viruses are able to produce the illness complex recognised as the common cold.

virus_list.name: Rhinovirus (HRV)
virus_list.classification: Species A, B, C with more than 100 serotypes
virus_list.frequency_of_colds: more than 50% of all adult colds
virus_list.severity: usually mild, rarely causes lower respiratory disease in healthy adults
notes: Most common cause of common cold worldwide
More than 100 serotypes identified
Can be considered the most common infection of humans globally
Enters cells via ICAM-1 receptor on nasopharyngeal epithelium
Causes minimal nasal mucosa disruption but consistent nasopharyngeal damage
In children, a significant trigger for asthma exacerbations

virus_list.name: Seasonal Coronavirus
notes: Produces clinical picture similar to rhinovirus
More likely to produce myalgias, headaches, and malaise than rhinoviruses
More commonly produces fever than rhinovirus
With increasing immunity to SARS-CoV-2 worldwide, COVID-19 may eventually evolve to cause a common cold-like illness

virus_list.name: Respiratory Syncytial Virus
notes: Causes mild cold-like symptoms in older children and adults
A major cause of bronchiolitis and lower respiratory tract infections in infants under 2 years
RSV type A associated with more severe infections
In 2015, estimated 33.1 million episodes globally in children under 5, causing 3.2 million hospital admissions and over 11,800 deaths
Significant cause of morbidity and mortality in the elderly (estimated 1.2 million deaths in elderly from RSV and other respiratory viruses in 2015)
Immunity to RSV is short-lived, explaining repeated infections throughout life
RSV vaccine (Abrysvo) was approved by FDA in May 2023 for individuals 60 years and older

virus_list.name: Parainfluenza Virus
notes: Causes croup and bronchiolitis pattern in young children
Milder cold symptoms in older individuals and adults
Produces more fever than rhinovirus or RSV
12% of isolates in younger population, 2–7.5% in older population in studies

virus_list.name: Influenza Virus
notes: Usually produces a pattern of respiratory illness distinctly different from the common cold
Flu causes high fever, headache, body aches — unlike the milder nasal-centred cold
Third most common cause in some community studies
Key clinical distinction: influenza has high fever and myalgia; cold does not

virus_list.name: Adenovirus
virus_list.serotypes: 41 recognized serotypes with more than 100 subtypes
notes: Well known for producing conjunctivitis and laryngitis alongside cold symptoms
Types 3 and 7 cause pharyngoconjunctival fever — severe conjunctivitis and pharyngitis with minor cold symptoms
Pharyngoconjunctival fever most often found in summer when swimming in non-chlorinated pools
Genetic heterogeneity of adenoviruses makes population studies difficult

virus_list.name: Human Metapneumovirus
notes: Discovered in 2001 by researchers in the Netherlands in stored nasopharyngeal samples from children
Had been in circulation for approximately 65 years before discovery
Nearly every child is infected by age 5
Can cause severe lower respiratory illness in infants and immunocompromised individuals

virus_list.name: Human Bocavirus
notes: Discovered in 2005 from nasopharyngeal samples in children
Shown to cause common cold in children

virus_list.name: Echovirus
notes: Causes coryza — acute rhinitis with minimal other symptoms
Associated with summer cold-like episodes

virus_list.name: Coxsackievirus
notes: Well known for causing epidemic cervical myalgia, pleurisy, hand-foot-mouth disease, and herpangina alongside respiratory infections
Coxsackievirus type A21 can be transmitted via airborne droplets across a room
Associated with summer cold outbreaks

virus_list.name: SARS-CoV-2 (Pandemic Coronavirus)
notes: Can cause cold-like symptoms especially with high population immunity
Pandemic caused by SARS-CoV-2 led to a revolution in respiratory virus research
With increased global immunity, COVID-19 may evolve toward a common cold pattern

virus_list.name: Enterovirus D68
notes: Associated with respiratory illness and potential severe neurological complications
Listed by CDC as a cause of cold-like symptoms in the United States

epidemiology.global_frequency: The most frequent acute illness in the United States and throughout the industrialized world

incidence_by_age.note: Incidence inversely related to age due to accumulating immunity from repeated exposures

seasonality.peak_seasons: autumn and winter in temperate climates
reason_for_winter_peak: people spend more time indoors in close contact with others
cold air may impair local nasal defences by slowing mucociliary clearance
reduced vitamin D levels in winter may affect immune function
lower humidity may favour virus survival

transmission_routes.primary: direct hand-to-hand contact — transfer of virus from infected person's hands to mucous membranes of susceptible person
transmission_routes.tertiary: inhalation of respiratory aerosol droplets from coughing or sneezing within close range
transmission_routes.droplet_route: possible when infected person coughs or sneezes and recipient is within a few feet
transmission_routes.kissing: low risk — only 1 of 16 susceptible recipients infected in a study of 1.5-minute kisses; saliva has little detectable virus 90% of the time
transmission_routes.recirculated_air: studies of commercial airliners show no difference in cold incidence with recirculated vs fresh air ventilation

contagiousness_period.peak: second day of illness when viral shedding is highest
contagiousness_period.duration: low level viral shedding may persist for up to 2 weeks
contagiousness_period.incubation_note: virus present in nasal washings during incubation period before symptoms begin

epidemiology.special_transmission_note: The family is the major site for spread of rhinoviruses. The pool of infected donors is often the school population. Virus is then brought home and spread through the family.

incubation_period.note: Symptoms usually show up approximately 2 days after a person becomes infected

symptom_duration.extended_cases: up to 2–3 weeks in some people
symptom_duration.rapid_resolution_possible: the cold may abort after only 1 day

specific_symptom_timeline.cough_nasal_discharge_postnasal_drip_thr: may still be present on day 14 after onset

common_symptoms.details: Initially clear and watery during first 2 days, then becomes more viscous and mucopurulent. The most common symptom of the common cold.
common_symptoms.mechanism: Bradykinin-induced nasal blood vessel dilation and increased glandular secretion

common_symptoms.details: Stuffiness due to swelling and oedema of the nasal mucosa. Second most common symptom.
common_symptoms.mechanism: Inflammatory mediators causing vasodilatation and mucosal swelling

common_symptoms.details: Often one of the earliest symptoms, frequently occurring in the first 1–2 days
common_symptoms.mechanism: Bradykinin and prostaglandin stimulation of nasal nerve endings

common_symptoms.details: Common early symptom, typically mild. Often the very first sign of a developing cold. Decreases after day 2–3.
common_symptoms.mechanism: Bradykinin activating pain nerve endings in the throat

common_symptoms.details: Usually mild; caused mainly by nasal obstruction and postnasal drip stimulating upper airway cough receptors. In young children RSV and parainfluenza can cause cough by direct lower respiratory tract invasion.
common_symptoms.mechanism: Postnasal drip stimulation of pharyngeal cough receptors; prostaglandins increase cough reflex sensitivity

common_symptoms.details: Common, especially in early cold. More severe headache may suggest influenza.
common_symptoms.mechanism: Prostaglandin E2 mediates headache; cytokine-induced systemic inflammation

common_symptoms.details: Temperature below 38°C (100.4°F). Uncommon in adults but may be present in children. High fever is NOT typical of the common cold — it suggests influenza or another diagnosis.
common_symptoms.mechanism: Cytokine IL-6, IL-8, TNF-alpha stimulate prostaglandin-mediated fever

common_symptoms.symptom: Mild body aches and muscle pain (myalgia)
common_symptoms.details: Mild muscle and joint aches. Severe myalgia is more characteristic of influenza.
common_symptoms.mechanism: Cytokine-induced systemic inflammation; prostaglandin E2 mediates muscle pain

common_symptoms.details: Feeling of illness and lethargy
common_symptoms.mechanism: Systemic cytokine effects including IL-6 and TNF-alpha

common_symptoms.details: May appear early in the illness; virus can travel via tear ducts from eyes into nasal cavity
common_symptoms.mechanism: Inflammatory response in conjunctiva

common_symptoms.details: Reduced desire to eat during active illness
common_symptoms.mechanism: Cytokine-mediated appetite suppression

common_symptoms.details: Mucus dripping down the back of the throat; often contributes to persistent cough and throat clearing
common_symptoms.mechanism: Excess mucus production combined with impaired mucociliary clearance

mechanism_of_symptoms.overview: Viral infection of the upper respiratory tract triggers a local innate immune response in the infected epithelium. This response generates all the symptoms of the common cold through two pathways: systemic cytokine-mediated symptoms and local inflammatory mediator-driven symptoms.

systemic_pathway.trigger: Pattern Recognition Receptors (PRRs) on epithelial cells and immune cells detect viral DNA and RNA

local_pathway.bradykinin_mechanism: Generated by release of kallikrein enzyme from epithelial cells converting kininogen to bradykinin. Acts on blood vessels and nerves.
local_pathway.prostaglandin_mechanism: Arachidonic acid released from membrane phospholipids by viral infection is converted to prostaglandins by cyclooxygenase enzymes. Prostaglandin E2 is most common.
local_pathway.important_note: Histamine is NOT a major mediator of common cold symptoms — unlike in allergic rhinitis. Kinins are more closely associated with cold symptoms than histamine. This explains why non-sedating antihistamines are ineffective for colds.

mechanism_of_symptoms.prodromal_symptoms: The first signs of a cold include throat irritation, sneezing, chilliness, mild fever, and tiredness — symptoms that may become more severe as infection progresses.

asymptomatic_infection.definition: Subclinical infection — person is infected with virus but shows no symptoms
asymptomatic_infection.also_possible: Exposure to cold viruses without becoming infected at all
asymptomatic_infection.study_data: In a 2-year study, 69–74% of positive respiratory virus samples from healthy individuals were classified as asymptomatic

risk_factors.overview: The common cold is influenced by many biological, behavioural, environmental, and social factors. Risk factors affect both the incidence (how often you get colds) and the severity (how bad they are).

factors_increasing_incidence.details: Infants and children have undeveloped immune systems and have not yet acquired immunity through previous exposures. School-age children have 6–8 colds per year versus 2–4 for adults. Children in daycare or school settings have markedly increased exposure.
factors_increasing_incidence.mechanism: Immature immune system; no prior exposure to the many rhinovirus serotypes

factors_increasing_incidence.details: Long-term psychological stress negatively impacts the immune system and mucosal immunity. Studies show a moderate correlation between stressful life events and incidence of common cold. A 1-year study of 1,149 subjects aged 23–68 found psychological stress was a risk factor.
factors_increasing_incidence.mechanism: Stress suppresses secretory immunoglobulin A (sIgA); cortisol release may compromise immune response

factors_increasing_incidence.details: Poor sleep quality is an important predictor of cold susceptibility. Subjects with less than 7 hours of sleep were almost three times more likely to develop a cold than those with 8 or more hours, confirmed in multiple studies.
factors_increasing_incidence.mechanism: Sleep deprivation decreases mitogen proliferation of lymphocytes and affects multiple immune markers

factors_increasing_incidence.details: Spending time in crowds — underground trains, supermarkets, theatres, cinemas, restaurants, parties — increases risk of circulating respiratory infections. Paradoxically, very sociable persons may have greater resistance than introverted persons despite more exposures, though the mechanism is unknown.
factors_increasing_incidence.mechanism: Direct contact and close proximity facilitates viral transmission

factors_increasing_incidence.details: Smokers are more likely to develop infections after virus exposure and also more likely to develop illness compared to non-smokers. Smoking increases risk of respiratory infection.
factors_increasing_incidence.mechanism: Damages respiratory epithelium; alters structural, functional, and immunological host defences

factors_increasing_incidence.factor: Children in household or daycare settings
factors_increasing_incidence.details: Exposure to young children in daycare settings significantly increases cold risk. Women are almost twice as likely to develop a cold as men when children in the family are sick, because women have more contact with children.
factors_increasing_incidence.mechanism: Children are major virus shedders; close household contact increases transmission

factors_increasing_incidence.factor: No prior immunity to specific serotype
factors_increasing_incidence.details: Adults have fewer colds than children because they have accumulated partial immunity through exposure to many rhinovirus serotypes. However, with over 100 rhinovirus serotypes, complete immunity is never achieved.
factors_increasing_incidence.mechanism: Antibody-mediated protection against specific serotypes; each infection induces short-lived serotype-specific immunity

factors_increasing_incidence.details: More symptomatic infections in winter and during rainy season in tropics. People spend more time indoors in closer contact; cold inspired air may also slow mucociliary clearance and leukocyte activity.
factors_increasing_incidence.mechanism: Indoor crowding; cold air impairs local nasal defences; lower vitamin D in winter

factors_increasing_incidence.details: Deficiency of calories, protein, vitamins C and D, and minerals impairs general health and immune function. Malnourished children in developing countries are particularly susceptible to respiratory infection morbidity and mortality.
factors_increasing_incidence.mechanism: Nutrients support epithelial integrity and immune cell function

factors_increasing_severity: asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)

controversial_factor_cold_exposure.folk_belief: Getting chilled, going outside with wet hair, or getting caught in the rain causes colds
controversial_factor_cold_exposure.scientific_evidence: Laboratory experiments involving challenge with cold viruses and chilling have failed to demonstrate any effect of cold exposure on susceptibility to infection. Cold temperatures do NOT directly cause colds.
controversial_factor_cold_exposure.nuanced_explanation: There is a proposed mechanism: chilling of the body surface causes intense ischaemia and cooling of the pharynx and tonsils. This reflex vasoconstriction may reduce resistance to infection, potentially converting a subclinical infection into a symptomatic one. More people catch colds in cold weather because they spend more time indoors in prolonged contact with infected people — not because of the cold itself.
controversial_factor_cold_exposure.conclusion: Cold temperatures do not directly cause the common cold. The virus must be present.

alcohol_note.evidence: Moderate alcohol consumption (up to 3–4 drinks/day) was associated with decreased risk of developing a cold in non-smokers in one study. Moderate alcohol may have a beneficial effect on the immune system.
alcohol_note.caution: This does not constitute a recommendation to consume alcohol as prevention

pathophysiology.overview: The common cold is a syndrome of symptoms caused by the innate immune response to viral infection of the upper respiratory tract epithelium, not by direct tissue damage from the virus itself. Symptoms vary from person to person and depend on the infecting virus and the host's immune response.

viral_entry.rhinovirus_entry: Epithelial cells of the nasopharynx carry intercellular adhesion molecule-1 (ICAM-1) receptors. Rhinovirus binds these receptors to enter cells. Nasal epithelial cells do NOT have these receptors — explaining why rhinovirus causes minimal nasal mucosa destruction but consistent nasopharyngeal damage.
viral_entry.other_viruses: Different viruses use different entry mechanisms and receptors

inflammatory_cascade.step_1: Virus infects respiratory epithelium and replicates
inflammatory_cascade.step_2: Pattern Recognition Receptors (PRRs) detect viral RNA or DNA
inflammatory_cascade.step_4: Release of cytokines: interferons, IL-6, IL-8, TNF-alpha
inflammatory_cascade.step_5: Recruitment of immune cells (neutrophils, macrophages, lymphocytes)
inflammatory_cascade.step_6: Local inflammatory mediators generated: bradykinin, prostaglandins
inflammatory_cascade.step_7: Nasal blood vessel dilation, mucosal oedema, increased secretion
inflammatory_cascade.step_8: Systemic cytokine circulation producing fever, headache, myalgia, fatigue

nasal_mucosa_changes.rhinovirus_infection: Characterised by oedema and hyperaemia with transudative rhinorrhoea, WITHOUT direct damage to the columnar epithelium
nasal_mucosa_changes.influenza_contrast: Influenza, adenoviruses, and parainfluenza viruses cause more severe cytopathic effects on respiratory epithelium
sequence: Separation of epithelial cells by oedema fluid
Surface cells loosen and slough off
Entire epithelium may disintegrate in severe cases
Cell regeneration begins from basement membrane

mucopurulent_discharge.appearance: Yellow or green nasal discharge is NORMAL as the cold progresses
mucopurulent_discharge.cause: Influx of neutrophils and macrophages; does NOT indicate bacterial infection requiring antibiotics
mucopurulent_discharge.clinical_implication: Presence of coloured mucus is not a reason to prescribe antibiotics

eustachian_tube_effects.findings: 2 days after rhinoviral infection, eustachian tube function was reduced to 50% of usual potency in studies
eustachian_tube_effects.middle_ear_effect: 20% of infected persons had significant pressure changes in the middle ear
eustachian_tube_effects.implication: Creates conditions for secondary bacterial otitis media

clinical_diagnosis.basis: Symptoms and observed signs — no laboratory tests required for typical uncomplicated cases
physical_examination_findings: Swelling and congestion of nasal passages
Redness of the throat (mild, without exudate)
Possible enlarged lymph nodes in the neck
clinical_diagnosis.chest_xray: NOT needed unless chest exam is abnormal or pneumonia is suspected

conditions_that_mimic_cold.differentiator: Cough or sore throat usually NOT seen with allergies; itching is more prominent; symptoms are recurrent and triggered by allergens
Nasal congestion and drainage NOT generally seen; high fever; exudate on tonsils
Usually associated with significant facial pain and purulent nasal discharge lasting beyond 10 days without improvement
High fever (38–40°C), severe myalgia, headache, and rapid onset distinguish flu from cold. Rapid influenza test during flu season can confirm.
conditions_that_mimic_cold.rule: During flu season, obtain nasal swabs for rapid flu testing

conditions_that_mimic_cold.differentiator: Associated with prolonged coughing, sometimes with vomiting; characteristic whoop sound
May be indistinguishable from common cold especially with high immunity; testing required if antiviral treatment eligibility is relevant
Non-infectious, triggered by environmental factors; no fever, no infectious prodrome

laboratory_testing.when_indicated: Routine laboratory testing is NOT recommended for uncomplicated common cold
special_circumstances: Rapid influenza antigen test when influenza is suspected during flu season
Rapid RSV test for high-risk infants under 2 years with compatible symptoms
COVID-19 testing when antiviral treatment may be indicated
C-reactive protein (CRP) can help distinguish viral (CRP <20 mg/L) from bacterial infection (CRP >40 mg/L)

nucleic_acid_PCR.use: reference labs, research, returned travellers, low parasitaemia

serology.use: IgG antibody testing — can be done any time, not just during acute illness

tissue_culture.gold_standard_role: viral culture remains important gold standard despite advances in antigen detection

complications.overview: The common cold itself is of itself harmless in most cases, but bacterial invasion may follow the initial viral infection. These secondary invaders may produce disorders of serious consequence. All respiratory viruses are associated with causing common cold syndrome, but mild illness can develop into more serious lower respiratory tract infections.

complications_list.frequency: most common complication of the common cold
complications_list.mechanism: Cold causes problems with drainage and pressure regulation of the middle ear through eustachian tube dysfunction; allows secondary bacterial infection
complications_list.evidence: In one study, more than 90% of patients with otitis media had cold symptoms that were suspected to be virally induced; middle ear fluid contained culturable bacteria in 50–70% of cases

complications_list.mechanism: Viral sinusitis may be followed by secondary bacterial infection if mucociliary clearance is impaired
complications_list.note: Viral sinusitis (more common) will resolve within 3 weeks without antibiotics; bacterial sinusitis presents with worsening facial pain after initial improvement

complications_list.mechanism: Inflammation of the larynx (voice box) causing hoarseness or voice loss
Inflammation of the membrane lining the trachea (windpipe)
Inflammation of the bronchial membranes; may develop if virus spreads to lower airways

complications_list.frequency: mainly in infants under 2 years from RSV or parainfluenza
notes: RSV can infect lungs especially in children, older adults, and immunocompromised
In 2015: 33.1 million RSV-related episodes globally in children under 5, with 3.2 million hospital admissions and over 11,800 deaths

complications_list.mechanism: Barking cough and stridor from subglottic swelling
complications_list.cause: Primarily parainfluenza virus in young children

complications_list.note: Respiratory viruses previously believed restricted to upper airways are a common cause of lower respiratory infections

complications_list.frequency: rhinoviruses are a leading trigger for acute asthma attacks in children
complications_list.evidence: Rhinoviruses are responsible for considerable morbidity related to asthma exacerbation; airway hyperresponsiveness may persist up to 4 weeks post-infection
studies: Johnston SL et al (1995): community study in 9–11 year old children linking viral infections to asthma exacerbations
Tovey ER et al (2015): rhinoviruses significantly affect day-to-day respiratory symptoms in children with asthma

complications_list.mechanism: Respiratory viruses are major triggers for acute exacerbations of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and chronic bronchitis

serious_complication_warning_signs_requi: persistent high fever not responsive to paracetamol or ibuprofen
persistent or increasing shortness of breath
severe headache combined with neck pain or stiffness
dizziness, weakness, confusion, or constant lack of energy
signs_requiring_healthcare_provider_visi: coughing up thick grey or bloody sputum
development of even mild shortness of breath
worsening symptoms after a few days of getting better

treatment.principle: No cure exists for the common cold. No vaccines are currently available for the common cold. Treatments aim to relieve symptoms while the immune system clears the infection. The illness is self-limiting and will resolve on its own.

antibiotics.reason: Antibiotics work against bacteria, NOT viruses. They do not kill viruses and provide no benefit for uncomplicated colds.
risks_of_unnecessary_antibiotics: allergic reactions ranging from mild rash to severe anaphylaxis
Clostridioides difficile (C. diff) infection causing serious diarrhoea
GI symptoms including nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea
contribution to antibiotic resistance in community
antibiotics.exception: Antibiotics are appropriate only if a secondary bacterial infection develops (e.g., bacterial sinusitis, pneumonia, bacterial otitis media)

antiviral_therapy.common_cold_viruses: There are currently no antivirals that work against rhinoviruses or other common respiratory viruses causing cold symptoms
antiviral_therapy.covid_19: If COVID-19 is diagnosed, antiviral treatment (e.g., nirmatrelvir/ritonavir) may be available and should be started within 5–7 days of symptom onset
antiviral_therapy.influenza: Antivirals for flu work best when started within 2 days of symptom onset
antiviral_therapy.note: Contact healthcare provider promptly if symptoms could be COVID-19 or flu in high-risk patients

analgesics_antipyretics.paracetamol_dose: 500–1000 mg every 4–6 hours as needed while awake, with water (max 4000 mg/day)
analgesics_antipyretics.ibuprofen_dose: 200–400 mg every 6–8 hours as needed with small snack (max 1200 mg/day)
analgesics_antipyretics.ibuprofen_avoid_in: persons over 65, pregnant women, severe liver or kidney disease, peptic ulcer disease, heart failure, history of stroke, GERD, IBD, liver cirrhosis
analgesics_antipyretics.aspirin_note: Aspirin reduces some cold symptoms but increases viral shedding duration; not recommended in children due to Reye's syndrome risk

nasal_decongestants_topical.mechanism: Constrict nasal blood vessels, reducing mucosal swelling
nasal_decongestants_topical.critical_warning: Limit use to 2–3 days — rebound congestion (rhinitis medicamentosa) occurs after 72 hours of use; the congestion may worsen. Can also cause nosebleeds, agitation, insomnia, and worsened hypertension.
nasal_decongestants_topical.reasons_for_infant_contraindication: Risk of serious CNS effects ranging from sedation to convulsive attacks resembling seizures in infants and young children

nasal_decongestants_oral.efficacy: Pseudoephedrine effective; phenylephrine (common OTC ingredient) is NOT very effective
nasal_decongestants_oral.pseudoephedrine_note: Purchase limited due to use in manufacture of amphetamine drugs

first_generation.benefit: Modest benefit for sneezing and runny nose in adults
first_generation.mechanism_of_limited_benefit: Rhinorrhoea in colds is mediated by kinins, not histamine — antihistamines are not targeting the primary mediator
first_generation.antihistamine_for_cough: Thought to act indirectly by reducing postnasal drip
first_generation.note: Antihistamines may be helpful in adolescents and adults; NOT recommended in young children

second_generation.efficacy_for_cold: NOT effective for common cold symptoms
second_generation.reason: Second-generation antihistamines do not have the same anticholinergic properties; histamine is not the main mediator of cold symptoms

cromolyn_sodium.benefit: May relieve runny nose, cough, and sneezing

dextromethorphan.evidence: Conflicting results; more effective than codeine in studies
dextromethorphan.indication: May provide relief when persistent cough disrupts sleep or feeding
dextromethorphan.not_needed: Cough suppression is usually not needed; cough reflex is a protective mechanism

antitussives_cough_suppressants.antihistamines_for_cough: May reduce cough through drying effect on mucosa and reduction of postnasal drip

guaifenesin.evidence: One RCT in 65 young adults showed no change in cough or sputum thickness
guaifenesin.note: Despite popularity, evidence of benefit is limited

ipratropium_bromide_nasal_spray.evidence: 5 RCTs in adults showed significant symptom relief, especially for excessive nasal discharge and sneezing

lozenges.evidence: Some studies show reduction in duration and severity of cold symptoms when taken within 24 hours of symptom onset
lozenges.critical_warning: Intranasal zinc products have been associated with PERMANENT loss of smell — CONTRAINDICATED as nasal products
lozenges.child_evidence: Studies in children taking zinc sulfate decreased cold rate, but adult studies are inconsistent

vitamin_c.prevention: Does NOT reduce cold incidence in the general population — routine supplementation NOT justified
vitamin_c.treatment: If started after onset of cold symptoms, does NOT reduce symptom severity or duration
vitamin_c.regular_supplementation: May slightly reduce duration of colds if taken regularly before illness onset
vitamin_c.background: Claims that vitamin C prevents and cures colds were popularised by Nobel laureate Linus Pauling in 1970; later large meta-analyses found no benefit for prevention

vitamin_d.evidence: Controversial. Some reports show no benefit; others report benefit especially in vitamin D deficient individuals

echinacea.evidence: Two of the most popular herbal treatments with some support from clinical trials. Clinical relevance of efficacy has been questioned by Cochrane reviews. Some support from RCTs.

pelargonium.evidence: Some support from clinical trials for acute cough due to lower respiratory tract infection

iota_carrageenan.claimed_benefit: Antiviral medicine for common cold; studied in several clinical trials

intranasal_glucocorticoids.evidence: NOT effective for common cold symptoms; ARE effective for allergic rhinitis

age_restriction_otc.rule: Over-the-counter cough and cold medicines are NOT recommended for children younger than 6 years old
age_restriction_otc.reason: Can result in serious and sometimes life-threatening side effects
age_restriction_otc.US_FDA_position: OTC cough/cold medicines not recommended for children under 6
