fever_treatment_children.instruction: Contact healthcare provider about correct dose; read and follow all directions
fever_treatment_children.age_restriction_ibuprofen: Avoid in infants under 6 months without medical guidance

symptomatic_treatments_children.codeine_in_children: NOT recommended — risk of respiratory depression and narcotic dependency
symptomatic_treatments_children.topical_decongestants_infants: CONTRAINDICATED — risk of serious CNS effects including convulsions

honey_for_cough.efficacy: Safe and effective for cough relief in children 1 year and older
honey_for_cough.contraindication: Babies under 1 year should NOT be given honey — risk of infant botulism

symptomatic_treatments_children.combination_products: Combination products containing topical anaesthetic agents, mucolytics, antihistamines, oral decongestants, antitussives, and anticholinergics should be avoided in young children. The American Academy of Pediatrics advises against use of combination cough and cold remedies.

rest.recommendation: Get plenty of sleep. Adjust sleeping position to prop head up with pillows to help mucus drainage.
rest.rationale: Sleep is critical for immune function; adults with less than 7 hours sleep are nearly 3 times more likely to develop a cold

fluids.recommendation: Drink plenty of fluids — 8 glasses per day. Water and fruit juice are ideal. Warm fluids such as tea and soups are especially soothing.
fluids.honey_addition: Adding honey can relieve sore throats and coughs in adults and children over 1 year

humidifier.recommendation: Use a cool-mist humidifier or vaporizer to increase air moisture and ease breathing
humidifier.warning: Breathe some steamy air but NOT hot steam directly — hot steam can damage nasal passages and cause burns

saline_nasal.drops_and_sprays: Saline nose drops or sprays are safe and effective for clearing congestion, especially in infants and young children
saline_nasal.gargling: Gargling with salt water can help clear mucus and soothe sore throats — mix half teaspoon of salt in 8 ounces of warm water
saline_nasal.suction_bulb: For young children, use a rubber suction bulb to clear mucus from nasal passages

throat_lozenges.recommendation: Use throat lozenges or cough drops for sore throat relief
throat_lozenges.age_restriction: Do not give lozenges to children younger than 4 years old — aspiration risk

supportive_home_care.diet: Eat a healthy diet high in fresh fruits (berries, citrus) and vegetables (leafy greens, peppers, carrots) to support immune function
supportive_home_care.smoking: Limit smoking or vaping — these worsen symptoms and delay recovery

steam_inhalation.sitting_in_steam_shower: Sitting in a bathroom with steam from a running shower may relieve congestion
steam_inhalation.hot_steam_inhalation: NOT recommended — hot steam can damage nasal mucosa; double-blind RCT showed breathing steam demonstrated increased airway resistance and fourfold increase in side effects

chicken_soup.tradition: Reported positive effects attributed to mucolytic effects of vapours from hot soup; may also stimulate nasal mucus production and loosen respiratory secretions
chicken_soup.evidence: Traditional use and soothing effect support recommending warm teas or soups

treatment_categories.before_cold_immune_support: Vitamins, minerals, probiotics, herbal medicines — evidence for most is limited; market valued over $20 billion USD in 2021
treatment_categories.at_first_signs_antiviral: No proven over-the-counter antiviral for common cold viruses available
treatment_categories.during_cold_symptom_relief: Main category of treatment; see symptomatic treatments above

prevention.overview: No vaccine is currently available for the common cold. Prevention relies on hygiene measures to interrupt transmission, general immune health practices, and reducing exposure to infectious contacts.

handwashing.recommendation: Frequent handwashing with soap and water — the single most effective preventive measure
handwashing.rationale: Rhinovirus recovered from 40–90% of hands of persons with colds; virus can survive on hands for at least 2 hours
handwashing.alternative: Alcohol-based hand sanitiser when soap and water unavailable (though studies show alcohol gels may be less effective when virus spreads by aerosol route)

avoiding_face_touching.recommendation: Avoid touching eyes, nose, and mouth with unwashed hands
avoiding_face_touching.reason: These are the entry routes for cold viruses into the body; virus can reach the nose when eyes are rubbed because tear ducts connect eyes to nasal cavity

respiratory_etiquette.recommendation: Cough and sneeze into your elbow or a tissue; dispose of tissues immediately
respiratory_etiquette.face_masks: Use face masks when sick or around sick contacts

avoiding_close_contact.recommendation: Avoid close contact with people who have a cold
avoiding_close_contact.crowded_places: Reduce time in crowded indoor spaces during cold season

surface_disinfection.recommendation: Disinfect commonly touched surfaces (phones, doorknobs, desks) with approved disinfectants
surface_disinfection.evidence: Iodine or phenol/alcohol disinfectants can interrupt transmission of rhinoviral infections in studies

prevention.not_sharing: Do NOT share food, drinks, utensils, or personal items with sick individuals

sleep.recommendation: Get 7–8 hours of sleep per night
sleep.evidence: Poor sleep quality is an important predictor of cold susceptibility; less than 7 hours of sleep nearly triples cold risk

prevention.stress_management: Manage chronic stress — prolonged psychological stress impairs mucosal and cellular immunity

diet_and_exercise.diet: Maintain a healthy diet rich in fruits and vegetables to support immune function
diet_and_exercise.exercise: Moderate exercise claimed to have beneficial effects on immune system and association with fewer sick days. However, a meta-analysis of 11 trials could not confirm this, and more research is needed. Severe exercise can INCREASE cold incidence in athletes.

vaccines.common_cold: No vaccine available for common cold — the large number of rhinovirus serotypes makes a universal vaccine impractical
vaccines.influenza: Annual influenza vaccination reduces flu-related respiratory illness; does NOT protect against rhinovirus or other cold viruses
vaccines.RSV_elderly: RSV vaccine (Abrysvo, mRESVIA) approved by FDA in May 2023 for adults 60 years and older
vaccines.RSV_infants: Nirsevimab (Beyfortus) monoclonal antibody recommended for infants and young children to prevent severe RSV infection
vaccines.vitamin_supplements: Regular supplementation with vitamins C, D, and E have NOT been shown to decrease incidence of colds in general population

travel_precautions.airline_travel: Studies show no difference in cold incidence with recirculated vs fresh air in commercial airliners — air conditioning is NOT a cause of colds

infants_and_young_children.vulnerability: Infants start life with little immunity and high incidence of colds (6–10/year); maternal immunity from breast milk declines in first year

maternal_immunity.transfer: Immunoglobulins transferred via placenta and breast milk
maternal_immunity.duration: Declines in first year as infant ceases breastfeeding; immunoglobulins have relatively short half-life
maternal_immunity.covid_pandemic_effect: During COVID-19 pandemic, reduced circulation of common respiratory viruses led to lower antibody levels in maternal milk, contributing to RSV resurgence when restrictions were lifted

infants_and_young_children.otc_restrictions: OTC cough and cold medicines NOT recommended under 6 years due to serious side effect risk
treatment_options: paracetamol or ibuprofen for fever
saline nasal drops
honey for cough (over 1 year only)
fluids and rest
infants_and_young_children.complications_risk: Higher risk of otitis media, bronchiolitis, and croup

elderly.vulnerability: Waning immunity associated with old age leads to more severe outcomes from respiratory viruses
elderly.rsv_risk: RSV is a significant cause of morbidity and mortality in elderly, causing exacerbation of chronic respiratory and cardiac disease
elderly.mortality_risk: Elderly patients may die if cold-like symptoms are not distinguished from influenza

pregnant_women.treatment: Paracetamol is safe in all trimesters for symptom relief
pregnant_women.ibuprofen: Avoid in third trimester of pregnancy
pregnant_women.covid_flu_antivirals: Contact healthcare provider promptly if COVID-19 or flu is suspected — antiviral treatment may be available and is especially important in pregnancy

immunocompromised_patients.risk: Higher severity and risk of complications
immunocompromised_patients.common_cold_to_serious_illness: What is a mild cold in healthy individuals can progress to pneumonia or severe lower respiratory disease in immunocompromised patients

asthma_patients.rhinovirus_risk: Rhinovirus infection is a major trigger for acute asthma attacks in children
asthma_patients.airway_hyperresponsiveness: May persist up to 4 weeks after a cold
asthma_patients.management: Worsening asthma with colds requires healthcare provider visit

parenthood_effect.finding: Parenthood has been reported to DECREASE the chance of developing cold symptoms when challenged with a common cold virus. There was a clear increase in protection with having more children in the family.
parenthood_effect.mechanism: Unknown — the resistance was independent of pre-challenge viral-specific immunity, suggesting a non-antibody-mediated protective mechanism

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is the common cold?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: The common cold is a mild, self-limiting viral infection of the upper respiratory tract — including the nose, sinuses, throat, and windpipe. It is caused by over 200 different viruses, most commonly rhinoviruses. It is the most frequent acute illness in humans, with adults averaging 2–4 colds per year and young children having 6–10 colds per year. Symptoms typically last less than a week and include runny nose, congestion, sore throat, sneezing, and cough.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Is there a cure or vaccine for the common cold?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: No. There is currently no cure and no vaccine for the common cold. Because colds are caused by over 200 different viruses — including more than 100 rhinovirus serotypes — developing a single vaccine is not practical. Treatment focuses entirely on relieving symptoms while the immune system clears the infection, usually within 7–10 days. Rest, fluids, and over-the-counter symptom relief medicines are the main approaches.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Do antibiotics help treat the common cold?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: No. Antibiotics only kill bacteria and have absolutely no effect on viruses. Using antibiotics for a cold provides no benefit and causes harmful side effects including diarrhoea, allergic reactions, and the development of antibiotic-resistant bacteria. Antibiotics should only be used if a secondary bacterial infection develops — such as bacterial sinusitis, ear infection, or pneumonia — which a doctor must confirm.

frequently_asked_questions.question: How does the common cold spread?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: The cold spreads primarily through hand-to-hand contact. When an infected person touches their own nose, they contaminate their hands, and when a susceptible person shakes that hand and then touches their own eyes or nose, the virus enters their respiratory tract. Viruses can also survive on surfaces for several hours. Breathing in aerosol droplets from an infected person's cough or sneeze is also a route of spread, though this requires close proximity. Kissing poses very low risk.

frequently_asked_questions.question: How is the common cold different from influenza (flu)?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Both are viral respiratory infections, but flu is generally much more severe. The common cold comes on gradually and mainly causes nasal symptoms. Flu comes on suddenly and is characterised by high fever (38–40°C), severe muscle aches, headache, and significant fatigue. Fever and myalgia are NOT typical of a common cold in adults. Flu is more likely to cause serious complications such as pneumonia. If you have severe systemic symptoms during flu season, see a doctor and ask about rapid influenza testing.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Can the same person get more than one cold a year?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Yes. Adults typically get 2–4 colds per year and children get 6–10. This is because there are over 200 cold viruses with more than 100 rhinovirus serotypes, and immunity to one strain does not protect against others. Also, immunity wanes after each infection. The same virus can cause another cold after re-exposure, though the second illness is usually milder.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Should I see a doctor for a cold?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Most colds do not require a doctor visit. However, seek emergency care if you have chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or confusion. See a healthcare provider if you have a fever lasting more than 5 days, symptoms worsening after initially improving, symptoms persisting more than 10 days without improvement, thick grey or bloody sputum, ear pain, or if you are at high risk from COVID-19 or flu — where antiviral treatment may be available and beneficial.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Are OTC cold medicines safe for children?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Over-the-counter cough and cold medicines are NOT recommended for children younger than 6 years old and can cause serious, sometimes life-threatening side effects. For fever, children can take paracetamol or ibuprofen. Honey (in children over 1 year), saline nasal drops, fluids, and rest are recommended safe options. Never give lozenges to children under 4 years old. Always consult a healthcare provider about the correct dose for children.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Does cold weather cause colds?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: No. Colds are caused by viruses, not cold temperatures. However, people tend to catch colds more often in cold weather because they spend more time indoors in closer contact with others, facilitating virus transmission. There is also some evidence that cold air may impair local nasal defences. But without exposure to a cold virus, cold weather alone cannot cause a cold.

frequently_asked_questions.question: How can I prevent getting a cold?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: The most effective prevention is frequent handwashing with soap and water for at least 20 seconds. Avoid touching your eyes, nose, and mouth with unwashed hands. Cough and sneeze into your elbow or a tissue. Avoid close, prolonged contact with sick people. Disinfect commonly touched surfaces. Do not share food or utensils. Get adequate sleep (7–8 hours) and manage stress. No vaccine or supplement has been proven to reliably prevent colds.

frequently_asked_questions.question: How long am I contagious when I have a cold?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: You are most contagious during the first 2–3 days of illness, when viral shedding is highest. However, low levels of virus can be shed for up to 2 weeks. You can also spread the virus in the incubation period (24–72 hours before symptoms begin). Good hand hygiene and covering coughs remain important throughout the illness and even before symptoms appear.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Can I go to work or school with a cold?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: If you feel well enough to carry out normal activities, it may be acceptable to go in, but take precautions to avoid spreading the virus. Practice meticulous hand hygiene, cover coughs and sneezes, and avoid touching your face. Consider staying home if symptoms are severe or if your workplace involves contact with vulnerable individuals (the elderly, immunocompromised patients, or infants).

frequently_asked_questions.question: Why do some people get more colds than others?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Several factors affect cold susceptibility: chronic psychological stress (triples risk), poor sleep (less than 7 hours nearly triples risk), smoking, crowded living or working conditions, young age, weakened immune system, and nutritional deficiency. Paradoxically, very sociable people who have many social contacts tend to have GREATER resistance to infection, possibly because frequent low-level exposures build broader immunity.

seek_emergency_care_immediately: Severe shortness of breath or persistent increasing shortness of breath
Severe headache combined with neck pain or stiffness (may indicate meningitis)
Severe weakness or inability to carry out normal activities
Signs of dehydration (no urination, sunken eyes, dry mouth)
Infants with fast breathing, chest indrawing, poor feeding, or bluish lips
Persistent high fever not responsive to paracetamol or ibuprofen
see_healthcare_provider_soon: Symptoms lasting more than 10 days without getting better
Symptoms improving then returning or worsening
Coughing up thick grey, yellow-green, or bloody phlegm
Chronic medical conditions that are getting worse
high_risk_groups_contact_provider_immedi: Older adults and pregnant women with any respiratory symptoms if COVID-19 or influenza suspected
Immunocompromised individuals with any respiratory symptoms
Infants under 3 months with any fever
Individuals eligible for antiviral treatment for COVID-19 or flu within first 5–7 days of symptoms

historical_overview.ancient_understanding: For centuries, the common cold was believed to be caused by chilling of the body. Greek and Roman physicians explained it through humoral pathology — chilling disturbing the humors and causing mucus to flow from the nose.
historical_overview.17th_century: Richard Lower, an eminent physician in London, published a treatise concluding that protection from external cold and proper perspiration prevented the disease.
historical_overview.1904: Bishop described the early manifestation of cold — dryness and irritation in the nose, leading to sneezing, copious mucus, lacrimation, and headache.
historical_overview.1930: Hilding identified two groups of colds: those due to exposure and those due to infection.
historical_overview.1944: Scientific consensus that the cause was a filterable virus, as determined by Krause in 1914 and later corroborated by Foster, Dochez and group.
historical_overview.1950s: Discovery of rhinoviruses by researchers provided the first scientific explanation for the common cold as an infectious viral disease.
historical_overview.1930s_1960s: Introduction of sulfa drugs in the late 1930s led some clinicians to claim antibiotics could treat colds — claims that were later disproven.
historical_overview.1970: Nobel laureate Linus Pauling published a book claiming vitamin C prevents and treats colds — a claim widely criticised as opinion-based but adopted by the general public.
historical_overview.2001_2005: Discovery of human metapneumovirus (2001) and human bocavirus (2005) as additional common cold pathogens.
historical_overview.2013: Cochrane meta-analysis of 29 trials on vitamin C concluded that routine supplementation is not justified for prevention in the general population.
historical_overview.2023: FDA approved first RSV vaccine for adults 60 and older.

history_and_science.common_cold_research_centre: The author of the Eccles 2023 review spent 30 years as Director of the Common Cold Centre at Cardiff University, UK, specialising in symptom mechanisms and treatments.

rhinovirus_biology.fastidious_subgroup: a subpopulation can only be cultured in living organisms, not reliably in tissue culture
rhinovirus_biology.animal_susceptibility: the only animal other than humans reliably infectable with rhinoviruses is the chimpanzee — a trivial human infection can be lethal to chimpanzees
rhinovirus_biology.temperature_sensitivity: rhinoviruses replicate at lower temperatures (33–35°C) which occur in the nasal passages, explaining their predilection for the upper airway

historical_transmission_study.location: Spitsbergen, a remote arctic archipelago, mid-point between Norway and North Pole
historical_transmission_study.findings: The isolated community had one attack of common cold per person per year. Epidemics of common cold never broke out before ships arrived each summer. In 1931, 48 hours after arrival of the first boat (which had one sailor with an incubating cold), three cases developed in the town — proving direct person-to-person transmission as essential.
historical_transmission_study.peak_cases: 26 cases peaked on day 10 after arrival, then tapered off over 3 weeks

economic_and_social_impact.antibiotic_misuse_consequence: Treating colds with antibiotics causes more harm than benefit and contributes to the growing global crisis of antibiotic resistance.

summary_profile.description: The common cold is a contagious viral infection of the upper respiratory tract — including the nose, sinuses, throat, and windpipe — caused by more than 200 different respiratory viruses, most commonly rhinoviruses. It is the most frequent acute illness in humans, with adults averaging 2–3 colds per year and young children experiencing 4 or more. There is no cure; the illness is self-limiting and typically resolves within 7–10 days, but it can cause serious complications such as pneumonia or bronchiolitis in vulnerable populations including infants, the elderly, and the immunocompromised.
common_symptoms: Runny nose (rhinorrhoea) — initially watery, later thick and discoloured
Sore or scratchy throat (often the first symptom, days 1–3)
Cough (usually mild; caused by postnasal drip)
Mild body aches and muscle pain
Low-grade fever (more common in children than adults)
Tickle or irritation in the throat (early sign, days 1–3)
severe_symptoms: High fever above 39°C (102°F) — suggests influenza or another serious infection, not typical cold
Severe or worsening shortness of breath or fast breathing
Extreme fatigue or inability to stay awake
Severe headache with neck stiffness (may indicate meningitis)
Blue or grey lips or fingernails (cyanosis) — emergency sign in children
Dehydration (no urination, dry mouth, sunken eyes)
Ribs showing with each breath in children
Fever in an infant younger than 2 months old (any temperature)
Ear pain or new hearing difficulty (possible otitis media)
Symptoms improving then returning or worsening (suggests secondary bacterial infection)
Cough persisting more than 3 weeks in children or more than 8 weeks in adults
causes: Rhinoviruses — most common cause; responsible for up to 50% of colds; over 100 serotypes
Common human coronaviruses (OC43, 229E, NL63, HKU1) — 15–21% of colds
Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) — also causes cold-like symptoms but is more likely to cause severe illness
Respiratory droplets released when an infected person coughs or sneezes — inhaled or deposited on mucous membranes of eyes, nose, or mouth
Direct contact with contaminated surfaces (fomites) — viruses survive on surfaces for several hours — followed by touching eyes, nose, or mouth
Close personal contact with an infected person (e.g., shaking hands)
risk_factors: Young age — children under 6 years get 4–10 colds per year due to immature immune systems and daycare/school exposure
Old age — waning immunity in elderly increases risk of severe outcomes
Weakened or compromised immune system (HIV/AIDS, chemotherapy, organ transplant)
Chronic conditions such as asthma, COPD, heart failure — increases risk of complications
Exposure to crowded settings — schools, daycares, offices, public transport, theatres
Smoking or vaping — damages respiratory epithelium and impairs local defences
Psychological stress — suppresses mucosal immunity (secretory IgA)
Insufficient sleep — less than 7 hours nearly triples cold susceptibility
Poor nutrition — deficiency of vitamins C and D and protein impairs immune function
Autumn and winter season — indoor crowding increases transmission; cold air may slow nasal defences
Lack of prior immunity to a specific virus serotype
Living with or caring for young children who attend school or daycare
diagnosis_methods: Clinical diagnosis — based on symptoms and physical examination alone in typical cases; no laboratory tests required
Physical examination: nasal swelling and congestion, mild throat redness without exudate, normal lung auscultation
Nasal or throat swab — to rule out influenza, COVID-19, streptococcal pharyngitis, or RSV when suspected
Rapid influenza antigen test (EIA/rapid flu test) — during flu season when influenza is suspected
Rapid RSV antigen test — for high-risk infants under 2 years with compatible symptoms
COVID-19 rapid antigen test or PCR — if COVID-19 is clinically possible, especially in high-risk individuals
Nasopharyngeal swab with PCR — for comprehensive respiratory virus panel; used in severe cases, immunocompromised patients, or hospitalised patients
Throat culture for Group A Streptococcus — to rule out bacterial strep throat when exudate or high fever is present
Chest X-ray — only indicated if pneumonia is clinically suspected (abnormal lung examination)
treatment_options: No cure exists for the common cold — treatment is entirely symptomatic and supportive
Rest — adequate sleep supports immune function and recovery
Hydration — 8 or more glasses of water, fruit juice, or warm fluids daily
Over-the-counter (OTC) pain relievers and fever reducers — paracetamol (acetaminophen) or ibuprofen for fever, headache, sore throat, and body aches
Saline nasal spray or drops — for nasal congestion relief; safe for all ages including infants
Nasal suction bulb — for clearing mucus in young infants and toddlers
Cool-mist humidifier or vaporizer — adds moisture to the air to ease breathing
Steam inhalation — sitting in a bathroom with steam from a running shower (do not use hot steam directly on face)
Throat lozenges or cough drops — for sore throat relief in adults and children 4 years and older
Honey — for cough relief in adults and children 1 year and older (do not give to infants under 1 year)
OTC decongestants (pseudoephedrine, oxymetazoline nasal spray) — short-term use for adults; NOT recommended for children under 6
OTC first-generation antihistamines (chlorpheniramine, diphenhydramine) — modest benefit for runny nose and sneezing in adults
OTC cough suppressants (dextromethorphan) — for troublesome cough in adults; NOT recommended for children under 6

Antiviral treatment for COVID-19 or flu — if COVID-19 or flu is diagnosed, antivirals (e.g., nirmatrelvir/ritonavir for COVID-19; oseltamivir for flu) must be started within 5–7 days for COVID-19 or 2 days for flu
Antibiotics — ONLY if a secondary bacterial infection is confirmed (pneumonia, bacterial sinusitis, bacterial otitis media); antibiotics have NO role in treating viral colds
medications: Paracetamol (acetaminophen) — 500–1000 mg every 4–6 hours as needed (max 4000 mg/day); for fever, headache, body aches, sore throat
Ibuprofen (NSAID) — 200–400 mg every 6–8 hours with food (max 1200 mg/day OTC); avoid in elderly, pregnant women, kidney or GI disease
Oxymetazoline nasal spray (Otrivin, Dristan) — topical decongestant; maximum 2–3 days use to avoid rebound congestion
Xylometazoline nasal spray — topical decongestant; maximum 2–3 days
Pseudoephedrine (Sudafed) — oral decongestant; use with caution in hypertensive patients
Phenylephrine — oral decongestant; commonly found in OTC products; limited clinical efficacy
Chlorpheniramine (Chlor-Trimeton) — first-generation antihistamine; modest benefit for sneezing and runny nose; causes drowsiness
Diphenhydramine (Benadryl) — first-generation antihistamine and antitussive; causes significant sedation
Doxylamine — sedating antihistamine; available in some combination cold products
Dextromethorphan (DM) — antitussive cough suppressant; for adults and children 12+ years
Guaifenesin (Mucinex) — expectorant; thins secretions to facilitate cough; limited evidence for benefit
Saline nasal spray or drops — safe, non-medicated; suitable for all ages including infants
Ipratropium bromide nasal spray — anticholinergic; reduces nasal discharge and sneezing in adults; evidence from 5 RCTs
Zinc gluconate lozenges — some evidence for reduction of cold duration if taken within 24 hours of symptom onset; do NOT use intranasal zinc (risk of permanent anosmia)
Cromolyn sodium nasal spray (NasalCrom) — may relieve runny nose and sneezing
Honey — for cough; effective and safe in children 1 year and older and adults
Nirmatrelvir/ritonavir (Paxlovid) — antiviral for COVID-19 if applicable; start within 5 days of symptom onset
Oseltamivir (Tamiflu) — antiviral for influenza if applicable; start within 48 hours of symptom onset
lifestyle_home_remedies: Get plenty of rest — allow the immune system to fight the infection effectively
Elevate head with extra pillows during sleep to ease nasal congestion and improve breathing
Drink 8 or more glasses of fluids daily — water, herbal tea, warm broths, or fruit juice
Drink warm fluids such as chicken soup, herbal tea with honey and lemon — soothes throat and loosens secretions
Use a clean cool-mist humidifier or vaporizer in your bedroom
Breathe steam from a bowl of hot water or a hot shower to ease congestion
Gargle with warm salt water — half teaspoon of salt in 8 ounces of warm water — for sore throat relief
Rinse nasal passages with saline drops or spray to clear congestion
Apply menthol vapour rub to chest and throat for temporary congestion relief in adults
Limit or avoid smoking and vaping — prolongs symptoms and impairs recovery
Wash hands frequently with soap and water for at least 20 seconds
Avoid touching eyes, nose, and mouth with unwashed hands
Cough and sneeze into a tissue or elbow and dispose of tissues immediately
Disinfect frequently touched surfaces (doorknobs, phones, keyboards)
Stay home and avoid close contact with others, especially vulnerable individuals
diet_recommended: Warm fluids — chicken soup, herbal teas, broths — help soothe symptoms and loosen secretions
Honey in warm tea or water — natural cough suppressant and throat soother (not for infants under 1 year)
Citrus fruits (oranges, lemons, grapefruits) — rich in vitamin C; supportive of immune function
Leafy green vegetables (spinach, kale) — rich in vitamins and minerals supporting immunity
Garlic — contains allicin; traditionally used for antimicrobial properties
Ginger — anti-inflammatory properties; soothes sore throat and nausea in warm tea
Yoghurt with live cultures — probiotics may support gut-immune axis
Water and clear fluids — maintain hydration; prevent dehydration especially with fever
Warm porridge or oatmeal — easy to swallow when throat is sore; provides energy
Bananas and soft fruits — easy to eat when appetite is reduced and throat is sore
diet_to_avoid: Alcohol — dehydrates the body and may impair immune function; avoid especially during active illness
Caffeinated beverages in excess — coffee, energy drinks, caffeinated sodas — can worsen dehydration
Dairy products (in some individuals) — may increase mucus thickness in certain people; consider reducing if mucus seems worse
Very spicy foods — may irritate an already inflamed sore throat
Cold, icy drinks — can worsen sore throat and throat irritation
Fried and heavily processed foods — high in saturated fat; may promote inflammation
Sugary foods and drinks — excess sugar may temporarily impair white blood cell immune function
Smoking and tobacco products — significantly worsen respiratory symptoms and impair recovery
complications: Acute otitis media (middle ear infection) — most common complication; especially in young children; caused by eustachian tube dysfunction allowing secondary bacterial infection
Acute bacterial sinusitis — rare; presents with worsening facial pain and purulent discharge persisting beyond 10 days without improvement
Viral sinusitis — more common than bacterial; typically resolves within 3 weeks without antibiotics
Bronchiolitis — infection of the small airways; mainly affects infants under 2 years from RSV; can require hospitalisation
Bronchitis — infection of the large airways; inflammation of bronchial membranes
Pneumonia — serious lower respiratory tract infection; more common in infants, elderly, or immunocompromised individuals
Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) — barking cough and stridor in young children; mainly caused by parainfluenza virus
Asthma exacerbation — rhinovirus infections are a leading trigger for acute asthma attacks in children; airway hyperresponsiveness may persist 4 weeks post-infection
Exacerbation of COPD or chronic bronchitis — respiratory viruses trigger acute exacerbations of chronic lung disease
Laryngitis — inflammation of the voice box causing hoarseness or voice loss
Worsening of other chronic medical conditions — including heart failure, COPD, and other chronic illnesses
Secondary bacterial infections — in rare cases viral infection precedes serious bacterial illness such as bacterial meningitis or sepsis
summary_profile.when_to_see_doctor: See a healthcare provider if you or your child has symptoms of a respiratory virus and is at higher risk of severe illness from COVID-19 or flu. Also see a provider if symptoms do not begin to improve within 10 days, if fever lasts longer than 4–5 days, if symptoms initially improve and then return or worsen (suggesting a secondary infection), if thick grey or bloody sputum is produced, if earache or sinus pain develops, or if you have chronic medical conditions such as asthma, COPD, diabetes, or heart disease that are getting worse. Infants under 3 months with any fever should be seen by a provider promptly.
emergency_signs: Trouble breathing or fast breathing in any age group
Severe shortness of breath or laboured breathing
Wheezing or noisy breathing (stridor)
Chest pain
Persistent high fever that does not respond to paracetamol or ibuprofen
Blue, grey, or pale lips or fingernails (cyanosis) — especially in infants and children
Ribs showing with each breath in a baby or child
Dehydration — no urination for 8 or more hours, dry mouth, sunken eyes, no tears when crying
Fever in an infant younger than 2 months old (any temperature requires emergency evaluation)
Confusion, unresponsiveness, or inability to be roused normally
Severe headache combined with neck stiffness and sensitivity to light (may indicate meningitis)
Baby or child appears to be getting noticeably sicker
Severe weakness or inability to stand or walk
Persistent vomiting preventing oral fluid intake
Symptoms suggestive of COVID-19 or influenza in a high-risk individual — contact provider immediately even with mild symptoms
